facts.fact_text: On 6 May 2012 the applicant was arrested during the dispersal of a political rally at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow.
On 23 April 2012 five individuals (Mr I. Bakirov, Mr S. Davidis, Ms Y. Lukyanova, Ms N. Mityushkina and Mr S. Udaltsov) submitted notice of a public demonstration to the mayor of Moscow.

The aim of the demonstration was to protest against abuses and falsifications in the course of the elections to the State Duma and of the President of the Russian Federation, and to demand fair elections, respect for human rights, the rule of law and the international obligations of the Russian Federation.

On 3 May 2012 the Moscow Department of Regional Security approved the alternative route from Kaluzhskaya Square, down Bolshaya Yakimanka Street and Bolshaya Polyanka Street, followed by a meeting at Bolotnaya Square.
The march began at 4.30 p.m. at Kaluzhskaya Square.
The march proceeded down Yakimanka Street peacefully and without disruption.
At approximately 5 p.m. the march approached Bolotnaya Square.

After around fifteen minutes of attempting to engage with the cordon officers, at 5.16 p.m. the four leaders (Mr S. Udaltsov, Mr A. Navalnyy, Mr B. Nemtsov and Mr I. Yashin) announced that they were going on a 'sit-down strike' and sat on the ground.
The leaders of the sit-in called on other demonstrators to follow their example and sit down, but only a few of their entourage did so (between approximately twenty and fifty people in total).
On 6 May 2012 the applicant arrived at Bolotnaya Square at around 6 p.m. to take part in the meeting.
The applicant stood in front of the stage on Bolotnaya Embankment, within the area designated as the meeting venue.
According to the applicant, between 6 p.m. and 7 p.m. the area around him remained peaceful, although there was general confusion.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly adopted by the Venice Commission at its 83rd Plenary Session (Venice, 4 June 2010) provided that an assembly should be deemed peaceful if its organisers have professed peaceful intentions and the conduct of the assembly is non-violent, and that the term 'peaceful' should be interpreted to include conduct that may annoy or give offence, and even conduct that temporarily hinders, impedes or obstructs the activities of third parties.
On 6 May 2012 the applicant was arrested during the dispersal of a political rally at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow.
The applicant was detained at the police station for at least thirty-six hours pending administrative proceedings.
The applicant was sentenced to fifteen days' administrative detention.
At 6.15 p.m., at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, the riot police began breaking into the demonstration to split the crowd.
Running in tight formations, the riot police pushed the crowd apart, arrested some people, confronted others and formed new cordons to isolate sections of the crowd.
The police applied combat techniques and used truncheons during the dispersal at 6.15 p.m.
The dispersal of the demonstration continued for at least another hour until the venue was fully cleared of all protesters.
On 6 May 2012 the applicant arrived at Bolotnaya Square at around 6 p.m. to take part in the meeting.
The applicant stood in front of the stage on Bolotnaya Embankment, within the area designated as the meeting venue.

The applicant claimed that he had heard the police orders made through a megaphone to disperse, but in the general commotion he was unable to leave immediately and remained within the authorised meeting area until 7 p.m., when he was arbitrarily arrested by the police dispersing the demonstration.
The police apprehended the applicant and took him to a police van, where he waited for an hour before it left Bolotnaya Square for the police station.
The applicant was charged with obstructing traffic and disobeying lawful police orders, an offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.

The applicant was found guilty of disobeying lawful police orders and was sentenced under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation to fifteen days' administrative detention.
The map published by the Moscow Department of the Interior on 5 May 2012 delineated the area allotted to the meeting, which included the park at Bolotnaya Square.
The map published by the Moscow Department of the Interior on 5 May 2012 marked access to the meeting through the park at Bolotnaya Square.
The security plan was a ninety-nine-page internal document which had not been disclosed to the public or to the organisers.
The adjacent park at Bolotnaya Square had to be cordoned off under the security plan.
Unlike on 4 February 2012, the park at Bolotnaya Square was excluded from the meeting venue on 6 May 2012, which was limited to Bolotnaya Embankment.
The cordon officers did not enter into any discussion with the protest leaders and no senior officer was delegated to negotiate.

During the period between 5.20 p.m. and 5.45 p.m., no senior police officers or municipal officials came to the site of the sit-down protest, and there was no direct communication between the authorities and the leaders of the sit-in.
At 6 p.m. Police Colonel A. Makhonin told Ms N. Mityushkina to make an announcement from the stage that the meeting was over.

Ms N. Mityushkina made the announcement from the stage that the meeting was over, but apparently her message was not heard by most of the demonstrators or the media reporters broadcasting from the spot.
The live television footage provided by the parties contained no mention of Ms N. Mityushkina's announcement that the meeting was over.

On 13 August 2012, following an enquiry from the Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation regarding publication of the maps of the assembly of 6 May 2012, the Moscow Department of the Interior replied that on 5 May 2012 it had published on its official website a notice on 'Safeguarding public order in Moscow during the public events on 6 May'.

The Moscow Department of the Interior stated that the notice published on 5 May 2012 included information on the route, the map of traffic restrictions and information concerning the location of the socio-political events, the security measures and the warning against any unlawful acts during the events.

The Moscow Department of the Interior stated that the pictures contained in the notice were schematic and showed the approximate route of the march as well as the reference place of the meeting – 'Bolotnaya Square' – indicated in the security plan.

After the working meeting on 4 May 2012, the Moscow Department of the Interior prepared a security plan and map providing for the park at Bolotnaya Square to be cordoned off with metal barriers and for the participants in the meeting to be accommodated on the road at Bolotnaya Embankment.

The Moscow Department of the Interior did not discuss the security maps and security plan with the organisers, as those documents were for internal use showing the placement of the police forces and setting out their tasks.

The Expert Commission noted that the police did not inform the organisers of the changes they had decided upon, and the organisers only became aware of the police-imposed changes to the event when they arrived at the site on the afternoon of 6 May 2012.
The applicant claimed that he had not heard any announcement of the termination of the meeting.
The applicant denied that he had received any warning or orders before being arrested.
According to the Government, the applicant was arrested at 8.30 p.m. at Bolotnaya Square because he was obstructing the traffic and had disregarded the police order to move away.
Police Officer Y.'s report contained a handwritten statement that on 6 May 2012 at 9.30 p.m., at 5/16 Bolotnaya Square, together with Police Lieutenant A., he arrested the applicant (Mr Frumkin).

The rest of Police Officer Y.'s report was a printed template stating that the applicant, acting in a group of citizens, took part in an authorised meeting, went out onto the road and thus obstructed the traffic, did not react to the multiple demands of the police to vacate the road, thereby disobeying a lawful order of the police, who were fulfilling their service duty of maintaining public order and ensuring safety, and thereby committed an administrative offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The statement on the administrative offence contained an identical text to the printed template but indicated that the applicant had been arrested at 8.30 p.m.
The 'reasons' section of the administrative detention order remained blank.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow rejected the applicant's argument that the police report and the police statement were inconsistent as regards the time of his arrest, finding that the correct interpretation was that the time of arrest had been 8.30 p.m. and the detention at the police station 9.30 p.m.

The Federal Law on assemblies, meetings, demonstrations, marches and pickets (no. FZ-54 of 19 June 2004, the Public Events Act) required that notification of a public event be filed by its organiser in writing with the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities no earlier than fifteen days and no later than ten days prior to the scheduled date of the event.

Section 12(1)(iii) of the Public Events Act required the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities, upon receipt of the notification of a public event, to appoint an authorised representative to assist the event organisers in conducting the event in accordance with the law, with the appointment to be formally made by a written decision sent to the event organiser prior to the scheduled date of the event.

Section 13(1) of the Public Events Act provided that the representative of the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities had the right to require the organiser of a public event to comply with the conditions for holding the event and to decide on the suspension or termination of the public event.

Section 13(2) of the Public Events Act required the representative of the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities to be present at the public event, to assist the event organiser in the conduct of the public event, and to ensure, jointly with the organiser and the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior, public order and the safety of citizens and compliance with the law during the event.

Section 14(1) of the Public Events Act required the chief of the department of the interior in charge of the territory or venue where the public event is intended to be held to appoint an authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior to assist the event organiser in maintaining public order and the safety of citizens, with the appointment to be formally made by a written decision.

Section 14(2) of the Public Events Act provided that the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior had the right to require the organiser to announce the closure of access to the event if the maximum capacity of the venue is exceeded, to require the organiser and participants to comply with the conditions for holding the event, and at the request of the event organiser to remove any citizens disobeying the organiser's lawful orders.

Section 15 of the Public Events Act provided that if during the holding of a public event there occurs, through the fault of the participants, a breach of lawful order which does not entail a risk to the life or health of the participants, the representative of the executive body may require the event organiser to remedy the breach, and if the breach is not remedied the public event shall be terminated in accordance with section 17 of the Public Events Act.

Section 16 of the Public Events Act provided that a public event may be terminated if the event has created a real danger for the life and health of citizens or for the possessions of individuals or legal persons, or if the participants have committed unlawful acts and the organisers have deliberately breached the provisions of the Public Events Act relating to the conditions for holding the event.

Section 17(1) of the Public Events Act provided that in the event that a decision to terminate a public event is taken, the authorised representative of the executive body shall order the event organiser to terminate the public event giving the justification, determine a time-limit for compliance, and if the organiser does not comply, address the participants directly and allow additional time for compliance.
Section 17(2) of the Public Events Act provided that in the event of non-compliance with the order to terminate a public event, the police shall take all necessary measures to terminate the event.

Section 17(3) of the Public Events Act provided that the procedure for termination set out in section 17(1) shall not apply if mass disorder, riots, arson attacks or other emergency situations occur, in which case the termination shall be carried out in accordance with the legislation of the Russian Federation.

Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that failure to obey a lawful order or demand of a police officer in connection with the performance of the officer's official duties relating to maintaining public order and security, or impeding the officer's performance of his or her official duties, shall be punishable by a fine of between RUB 500 and RUB 1,000 or by administrative detention for up to fifteen days.

Article 27.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that the escorting or transfer by force of an individual for the purpose of drawing up an administrative-offence report shall be carried out as quickly as possible and shall be recorded in an escort-operation report, an administrative-offence report or an administrative-detention report.

Article 27.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that administrative detention or short-term restriction of an individual's liberty may be applied in exceptional cases if necessary for the prompt and proper examination of the alleged administrative offence or to secure the enforcement of any penalty imposed, and that where the detained person so requests, his or her family, the administrative department at the person's place of work or study and his or her defence counsel shall be informed of his or her whereabouts.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that any prior restrictions should be formalised in writing and communicated to the organiser of the event within a reasonable timeframe, and that the relevant authorities must ensure that any restrictions imposed during an event are in full conformity with the law.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that any restrictions placed on an assembly should be communicated in writing to the event organiser with a brief explanation of the reason for each restriction, and that such decisions should be communicated within a reasonable timeframe sufficiently far in advance to allow judicial appeal before the notified date of the event.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that if dispersal is deemed necessary, the assembly organiser and participants should be clearly and audibly informed prior to any intervention by law enforcement personnel, and participants should be given reasonable time to disperse voluntarily before law enforcement officials intervene further.

On 26 April 2012 the Head of the Moscow Department of Regional Security, Mr A. Mayorov, informed the organisers that the requested route could not be allocated because of preparations for the Victory Day parade on 9 May 2012.

On 3 May 2012 the Moscow Department of Regional Security informed the Chief of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Mr V. Kolokoltsev, that a different group of organisers had submitted notification of another public event – a meeting at Manezhnaya Square – which the Moscow authorities had rejected.

The organisers of the rejected meeting at Manezhnaya Square had expressed their intention to proceed in defiance of the ban and to occupy the square from 6 to 10 May 2012, ready to resist the police if necessary.
The Moscow Department of Regional Security requested the Moscow Department of the Interior to safeguard public order in Moscow in light of the threatened unauthorised occupation of Manezhnaya Square.
At the working meeting on 4 May 2012, the organisers stated that the turnout could significantly exceed the expected 5,000 participants.
At the working meeting on 4 May 2012, the organisers were warned that exceeding the number originally declared would be unacceptable.
On 5 May 2012 the Moscow Department of Regional Security requested the Moscow City Prosecutor's Office to issue a warning to the organisers against exceeding the notified number of participants.

On 5 May 2012 the Moscow Department of Regional Security requested the Moscow City Prosecutor's Office to issue a warning to the organisers against erecting camping tents at the meeting venue, an intention allegedly expressed by the organisers at the working meeting.
The Moscow Department of Regional Security referred to information found on the Internet that the demonstrators would go to Manezhnaya Square after the meeting.

The security plan provided for security measures in Moscow city centre in view of the forthcoming authorised demonstration at Bolotnaya Square and anticipated attempts by other opposition groups to hold unauthorised public gatherings.

The security plan provided for an 8,094-strong crowd-control taskforce, comprising police and military, to police the designated security areas and to prevent unauthorised public gatherings and terrorist attacks.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 were instructed to search the demonstrators to prevent them from taking camping tents to the site of the meeting.
The adjacent park at Bolotnaya Square had to be cordoned off under the security plan.
At approximately 6 p.m. a Molotov cocktail was launched from the crowd at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge over the restored police cordon.
The Molotov cocktail landed outside the cordon and the trousers of a passer-by caught fire.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, from 5.58 p.m. to 7 p.m. persons on Malyy Kamennyy Bridge and Bolotnaya Embankment made attempts to break the cordon, and threw empty glass bottles, fireworks, chunks of tarmac and portable metal barriers at the police officers.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. necessary measures were taken to push citizens away from Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, Bolotnaya Embankment and Bolotnaya Street and to arrest those who resisted the most, during which twenty-eight police officers and military servicemen sustained injuries of various gravity, four of whom were hospitalised.
At the working meeting on 4 May 2012, the organisers stated that the turnout could significantly exceed the expected 5,000 participants.
At the working meeting on 4 May 2012, the organisers were warned that exceeding the number originally declared would be unacceptable.
The map published by the Moscow Department of the Interior on 5 May 2012 delineated the area allotted to the meeting, which included the park at Bolotnaya Square.
The map published by the Moscow Department of the Interior on 5 May 2012 marked access to the meeting through the park at Bolotnaya Square.
At approximately 1.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the organisers were allowed access to Bolotnaya Square to set up the stage and sound equipment.
The installation of the stage and sound equipment was delayed due to the police searches and arrests.
During the time of the equipment installation, communication between the organisers setting up the stage and those leading the march was sporadic.
The leaders of the march found that the layout of the meeting and the placement of the police cordon did not correspond to what they had anticipated.
Unlike on 4 February 2012, the park at Bolotnaya Square was excluded from the meeting venue on 6 May 2012, which was limited to Bolotnaya Embankment.

A cordon of riot police in full protection gear barred access to the park at Bolotnaya Square and continued along the whole perimeter of the meeting area, channelling the demonstration to Bolotnaya Embankment.
Further down Bolotnaya Embankment there was a row of metal detectors at the entrance to the meeting venue.
By approximately 5 p.m. on 6 May 2012, the stage had been erected at the far end of Bolotnaya Embankment and a considerable number of people had already accumulated in front of it.

Faced with the police cordon and unable to access the park, the leaders of the march – Mr S. Udaltsov, Mr A. Navalnyy, Mr B. Nemtsov and Mr I. Yashin – stopped and demanded that the police open access to the park.

According to the protesters, they were taken aback by the alteration of the expected layout and demanded that the police officers at the cordon move the cordon back to allow sufficient space for the protesters to pass and to assemble for the meeting.
The cordon officers did not enter into any discussion with the protest leaders and no senior officer was delegated to negotiate.

Between 5.20 p.m. and 5.45 p.m. two State Duma deputies, Mr G. Gudkov and Mr D. Gudkov, contacted unidentified senior police officers to negotiate the enlargement of the restricted area by moving the police cordon behind the park along the lines expected by the organisers.

Mr V. Lukin, the Ombudsman of the Russian Federation, at the request of Police Colonel V. Biryukov, attempted to convince the leaders of the sit-in to resume the procession and to head towards the meeting venue at Bolotnaya Embankment, where the stage had been set up.

During the period between 5.20 p.m. and 5.45 p.m., no senior police officers or municipal officials came to the site of the sit-down protest, and there was no direct communication between the authorities and the leaders of the sit-in.
At 5.50 p.m. the crowd around the sit-down protest built up, which caused some congestion, and the leaders abandoned the protest and headed towards the stage, followed by the crowd.
At approximately 5.55 p.m. a commotion arose near the police cordon at the place vacated by the sit-down protest, and the police cordon was broken in several places.
A crowd of around a hundred people spilled over to the empty space beyond the cordon after it was broken.
Within seconds the police restored the cordon, which was reinforced by additional riot police.
The police cordon began to push the crowd into the restricted area and advanced by several metres, pressing it inwards.
At 6 p.m. Police Colonel A. Makhonin told Ms N. Mityushkina to make an announcement from the stage that the meeting was over.

Ms N. Mityushkina made the announcement from the stage that the meeting was over, but apparently her message was not heard by most of the demonstrators or the media reporters broadcasting from the spot.
The live television footage provided by the parties contained no mention of Ms N. Mityushkina's announcement that the meeting was over.
At 6.15 p.m., at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, the riot police began breaking into the demonstration to split the crowd.
Running in tight formations, the riot police pushed the crowd apart, arrested some people, confronted others and formed new cordons to isolate sections of the crowd.
The police applied combat techniques and used truncheons during the dispersal at 6.15 p.m.
At 6.20 p.m. many people were assembled in front of the stage, but the sound equipment had been disconnected.

Mr S. Udaltsov took a loudspeaker and addressed the crowd, calling for an indefinite protest action and stating that they would not leave until their comrades had been released, until the inauguration had been cancelled and until they were given airtime on the central television channels.
At 6.21 p.m. several police officers arrested Mr S. Udaltsov and took him away from the stage.
Mr A. Navalnyy attempted to go up onto the stage, but he was also arrested at the stairs and taken away.
At 6.25 p.m. the police arrested Mr B. Nemtsov, who had also attempted to address people from the stage.
At Malyy Kamennyy Bridge the police continued dividing the crowd and began pushing some sections away from the venue.
Through the loudspeakers the police requested that the participants leave for the metro station.
The dispersal of the demonstration continued for at least another hour until the venue was fully cleared of all protesters.

After the working meeting on 4 May 2012, the Moscow Department of the Interior prepared a security plan and map providing for the park at Bolotnaya Square to be cordoned off with metal barriers and for the participants in the meeting to be accommodated on the road at Bolotnaya Embankment.

The Moscow Department of the Interior did not discuss the security maps and security plan with the organisers, as those documents were for internal use showing the placement of the police forces and setting out their tasks.

The Expert Commission noted that on the evening of 5 May 2012 the police cordoned off the public gardens at Bolotnaya Square, according to Police Colonel Y. Zdorenko, in order to prevent the participants from setting up camp and from other illegal acts.

The Expert Commission noted that the authorities received information that the protesters might attempt to establish a protest camp at the site, causing them to decide that the rally should be confined to only the Bolotnaya waterfront area – a much smaller area than had been originally allocated for the assembly.

The Expert Commission noted that the police did not inform the organisers of the changes they had decided upon, and the organisers only became aware of the police-imposed changes to the event when they arrived at the site on the afternoon of 6 May 2012.

The Expert Commission's report stated that as the march approached Bolotnaya Square, demonstrators found that a police cordon was blocking off most of the square, leaving only a narrow stretch along the waterfront for the rally.

The Expert Commission's report stated that by 5.15 p.m. the majority of the march was immobile, and a number of leaders including Mr S. Udaltsov, Mr A. Navalnyy and Mr I. Yashin encouraged demonstrators to sit down on the road in front of the 'Udarnik' cinema facing the police cordon.

The Expert Commission's report stated that an estimated 50-200 people joined the sit-down protest, and the leaders stressed the need to maintain a peaceful protest and appealed to demonstrators to remain calm.

The Expert Commission's report stated that some demonstrators tried to pass through the police cordon to leave the area, but the police refused to let them through and directed them to go back through the crowd to Bolshaya Polyanka Street, even though this was practically impossible.

The Expert Commission's report stated that the police used loudspeakers to inform demonstrators of the rally location and asked participants to pass directly to Bolotnaya Square, but given the poor quality of the sound equipment, only those nearest the police could hear this information.

The Expert Commission's report stated that from the moment difficulties first arose for demonstrators attempting to cross Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, demonstrators made repeated attempts to negotiate with the police over moving their cordons to allow protesters onto Bolotnaya Square.

The Expert Commission's report stated that Mr D. Oreshkin, a member of the Presidential Human Rights Council, and State Duma deputy Mr G. Gudkov tried to talk to the police authorities at around 5.30 p.m., but there was no response.

The Expert Commission's report quoted organiser Ms N. Mityushkina as stating that she tried unsuccessfully to find the responsible people in the Ministry of the Interior to solve organisational problems, and that only at 6.00-6.30 p.m. did a senior police officer approach her and tell her that the authorities had suspended the demonstration and ask her to announce from the stage that the event was over.

The Expert Commission's report quoted organiser Mr S. Davidis as stating that he personally did not meet nor have time to get into contact with the authorities regarding the fences set up around the perimeter of the rally, and that he only saw OMON officers who behaved aggressively and were not predisposed to get into a conversation.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at 5.55 p.m. as people tried to move through the narrow gap between the police cordon and the waterfront, the police line moved two steps forward, further pressing the crowd, which generated a counter response from the crowd, and in several places the police cordon broke.

The Expert Commission's report stated that it was impossible to determine whether the breaking of the cordon was the result of conscious action by sections of the crowd or if the police cordon simply broke due to the pressure from such a large number of people.

The Expert Commission's report stated that in the two hours between 6 p.m. and 8 p.m. there does not appear to have been any clear reason for the police decision to advance other than to divide the crowd up into smaller sections, and that there is little evidence that demonstrators initiated the violence.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at around 6.20 p.m. the police announced that the rally was cancelled and asked protesters to disperse, but the announcement was not loud enough to reach the majority of the crowd.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at the same time as the dispersal announcement, Police Colonel V. Biryukov, head of the Moscow Department of the Interior's press service, told a group of human rights defenders that the demonstrators could continue to Bolotnaya Square to take part in the rally.

The Expert Commission's report stated that around 6.54 p.m. the police cordon that acted as a barrier along the waterfront near Luzhkov Bridge was removed, and demonstrators were able to move freely along the Bolotnaya waterfront.

The Expert Commission's report stated that approximately 15 minutes after 6.54 p.m., some 200 police officers in protective equipment began pushing protesters in the direction of Lavrushinsky Lane and back along the Bolotnaya waterfront from Luzhkov Bridge towards the Udarnik cinema.
The Expert Commission's report stated that at around 7.47 p.m. authorities created a corridor to allow demonstrators to leave the Bolotnaya area.
The Expert Commission's report stated that at 7.53 p.m. a group of OMON officers appeared from the bushes of Bolotnaya Gardens and divided those demonstrators that remained on the square.
The Expert Commission's report stated that at 8.08 p.m. the last groups of people slowly left the waterfront along a corridor formed by the policemen.

Ms S. testified that at 9.03 p.m. on 6 May 2012 she had been at Bolotnaya Square; the site had been fully cordoned off and the traffic had not resumed.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly adopted by the Venice Commission at its 83rd Plenary Session (Venice, 4 June 2010) provided that an assembly should be deemed peaceful if its organisers have professed peaceful intentions and the conduct of the assembly is non-violent, and that the term 'peaceful' should be interpreted to include conduct that may annoy or give offence, and even conduct that temporarily hinders, impedes or obstructs the activities of third parties.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that the policing of assemblies must be guided by the human rights principles of legality, necessity, proportionality and non-discrimination, and that the State has a positive duty to take reasonable and appropriate measures to enable peaceful assemblies to take place without participants fearing physical violence.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that if a standoff or other dispute arises during the course of an assembly, negotiation or mediated dialogue may be an appropriate means of trying to reach an acceptable resolution.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that no additional restrictions should be imposed by law enforcement personnel during an assembly unless absolutely necessary in light of demonstrably changed circumstances, and that the detention of participants during an assembly should meet a high threshold and should be used only in the most pressing situations when failure to detain would result in the commission of serious criminal offences.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that law enforcement agencies should be proactive in engaging with assembly organizers, that there should be a nominated point of contact within the law enforcement agency whom protesters can contact before or during an assembly, and that the policing operation should be characterized by a policy of 'no surprises'.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that law enforcement officials should differentiate between peaceful and non-peaceful participants, and that neither isolated incidents of sporadic violence nor the violent acts of some participants are themselves sufficient grounds to impose sweeping restrictions on peaceful participants in an assembly.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that so long as assemblies remain peaceful, they should not be dispersed by law enforcement officials, and that dispersal of assemblies should be a measure of last resort.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that dispersal should not occur unless law enforcement officials have taken all reasonable measures to facilitate and protect the assembly from harm and unless there is an imminent threat of violence.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that if dispersal is deemed necessary, the assembly organiser and participants should be clearly and audibly informed prior to any intervention by law enforcement personnel, and participants should be given reasonable time to disperse voluntarily before law enforcement officials intervene further.

On 4 May 2012 the deputy mayor of Moscow, Mr A. Gorbenko, ordered the Moscow Department of Regional Security to inform the organisers that their assembly notice had been accepted and to monitor its implementation.
Other public agencies were assigned the duties of street cleaning, traffic control and ensuring the presence of ambulances at the site of the assembly on 6 May 2012.

The Chief of the Tsentralnyy district of Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Major-General V. Paukov, was required to prepare, together with the organisers, the text of the public announcement to be made if the situation deteriorated.

The head of the Department for Liaison with Civil Society of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Internal Service Colonel V. Biryukov, had to ensure coordination with the representatives of public organisations and coordination and information flow with other services of the Moscow Department of the Interior.

After the working meeting on 4 May 2012, the Moscow Department of the Interior prepared a security plan and map providing for the park at Bolotnaya Square to be cordoned off with metal barriers and for the participants in the meeting to be accommodated on the road at Bolotnaya Embankment.

The Moscow Department of the Interior did not discuss the security maps and security plan with the organisers, as those documents were for internal use showing the placement of the police forces and setting out their tasks.

The Expert Commission noted that the police did not inform the organisers of the changes they had decided upon, and the organisers only became aware of the police-imposed changes to the event when they arrived at the site on the afternoon of 6 May 2012.
The Expert Commission noted that the City Council of Moscow did not send out a written announcement that a special representative from the city authorities would be present at the event.

The Expert Commission noted that the chairman of the Moscow local department of the Ministry of the Interior, Mr V. Kolokoltsev, did not issue any special orders on sending a special representative of the Ministry to the event.

The Expert Commission's report stated that from the moment difficulties first arose for demonstrators attempting to cross Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, demonstrators made repeated attempts to negotiate with the police over moving their cordons to allow protesters onto Bolotnaya Square.

The Expert Commission's report stated that Mr D. Oreshkin, a member of the Presidential Human Rights Council, and State Duma deputy Mr G. Gudkov tried to talk to the police authorities at around 5.30 p.m., but there was no response.

The Expert Commission's report quoted organiser Ms N. Mityushkina as stating that she tried unsuccessfully to find the responsible people in the Ministry of the Interior to solve organisational problems, and that only at 6.00-6.30 p.m. did a senior police officer approach her and tell her that the authorities had suspended the demonstration and ask her to announce from the stage that the event was over.

The Expert Commission's report quoted organiser Mr I. Bakirov as stating that a police officer in a colonel's uniform contacted him only once, and that later when clashes with the police erupted he could not find anyone with whom to communicate and cooperate.

The Expert Commission's report quoted organiser Mr S. Davidis as stating that he personally did not meet nor have time to get into contact with the authorities regarding the fences set up around the perimeter of the rally, and that he only saw OMON officers who behaved aggressively and were not predisposed to get into a conversation.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that no authorities were present on the spot and it was impossible to understand who was in command, and that State Duma deputies present on the spot tried to act as negotiators but said that nobody wanted to come up to them.
Mr S. Davidis testified that the police officers did not answer phone calls and he did not manage to find anyone in charge of the police.
Ms N. Mirza testified that Police Colonel V. Biryukov told her that he could do nothing, that he was not in charge of the riot police and that the riot police reported to the federal police.

Mr N. Svanidze testified that he asked why the passage would not be opened, but Police Colonel V. Biryukov kept turning his face away and would not answer, and Mr Svanidze understood that there was no point talking to him as he was not in command.
Mr N. Svanidze testified that neither the Ombudsman nor anyone else was able to get the passage widened despite requesting it.

Mr Vasilyev testified that the Ombudsman told Police Colonel V. Biryukov to let the cordon be moved back so that people could pass, but Police Colonel V. Biryukov told him that it was outside his powers and that he did not know in whose powers it was, at which point the police began breaking the crowd up.

Section 12(1)(iii) of the Public Events Act required the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities, upon receipt of the notification of a public event, to appoint an authorised representative to assist the event organisers in conducting the event in accordance with the law, with the appointment to be formally made by a written decision sent to the event organiser prior to the scheduled date of the event.

Section 12(1)(v) of the Public Events Act required the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities to ensure, within its competence and jointly with the organiser and the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior, public order and the safety of citizens during the public event and, if necessary, to provide them with urgent medical aid.

Section 13(2) of the Public Events Act required the representative of the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities to be present at the public event, to assist the event organiser in the conduct of the public event, and to ensure, jointly with the organiser and the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior, public order and the safety of citizens and compliance with the law during the event.

Section 14(1) of the Public Events Act required the chief of the department of the interior in charge of the territory or venue where the public event is intended to be held to appoint an authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior to assist the event organiser in maintaining public order and the safety of citizens, with the appointment to be formally made by a written decision.

Section 14(3) of the Public Events Act required the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior to facilitate the conduct of the public event and to ensure, jointly with the organiser and the executive body, public order and the safety of citizens and compliance with the law during the public event.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that the policing of assemblies must be guided by the human rights principles of legality, necessity, proportionality and non-discrimination, and that the State has a positive duty to take reasonable and appropriate measures to enable peaceful assemblies to take place without participants fearing physical violence.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that if a standoff or other dispute arises during the course of an assembly, negotiation or mediated dialogue may be an appropriate means of trying to reach an acceptable resolution.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that governments must ensure that law enforcement officials receive adequate training in the policing of public assemblies, including soft skills such as negotiation and mediation.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that law enforcement agencies should be proactive in engaging with assembly organizers, that there should be a nominated point of contact within the law enforcement agency whom protesters can contact before or during an assembly, and that the policing operation should be characterized by a policy of 'no surprises'.
